business_items.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
business_items.summary: Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.

Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”

“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”

Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

business_items.title: Trump says reported FBI database hack is ‘not good’
business_items.summary: The FBI is reportedly investigating a hack of the National Crime Information Center.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The FBI is reportedly investigating a hack of the National Crime Information Center.

The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), according to reports in CNN and the Associated Press .

The NCIC is the online database used by federal and local law enforcement to share information about warrants, background checks, and more. The scope of the breach does not yet appear to be clear.

A former FBI official told CNN that they’re not just concerned about “whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”

President Donald Trump addressed the reports during an interview Saturday with Fox News, saying, “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.” At the same time, Trump also said that as a result of the breach, “maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.”

In September, the FBI reportedly told agents and support staff that their personal information had been stolen in a cyberattack .

business_items.title: West Virginia Legislature hit with cyber incident affecting IT systems
business_items.summary: A cybersecurity incident that began Thursday was still ongoing Friday in the West Virginia Legislature. A spokesperson said the disruption did not spread to other government entities.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
A cybersecurity incident that began Thursday was still ongoing Friday in the West Virginia Legislature. A spokesperson said the disruption did not spread to other government entities.

West Virginia’s state legislature is responding to a cyberattack that has taken down its website and impacted IT systems.

Ann Ali, deputy chief of staff for the House of Delegates, told Recorded Future News that the attack started on Thursday and has continued through Friday.

“Upon discovery, the relevant teams immediately took steps to contain the incident and began an investigation with the help of outside cybersecurity specialists,” Ali said.

“In connection with the investigation, access to certain Legislature IT systems has been temporarily disabled. However, based on what we know so far, the incident appears to be limited to the Legislature’s computer systems.”

She added that no other state agencies or offices are impacted by the cyberattack. An investigation into the incident is ongoing but Ali did not respond to follow-up questions about whether it was a ransomware attack.

The West Virginia legislature is split between two bodies, a Senate and a House of Delegates with 134 total members representing the state’s 1.7 million residents. Multiple municipalities in the state have dealt with ransomware attacks in recent years, including the cities of Beckley and Westmoreland .

Security research firm Comparitech tracked 132 ransomware attacks on government bodies across the U.S. in the third quarter — a 91% increase compared to Q3 last year. At least 41 of the attacks involved U.S. based municipalities, including a major incident impacting Anne Arundel County in Maryland.

This week alone, residents of South Portland, Maine, lost access to critical city services due to a cyberattack , while Minnesota’s Otter Tail County notified its 61,000 residents of a data breach caused by a ransomware attack in July.

business_items.title: Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now
business_items.summary: Techies are building technology that can advance all aspects of the world — but can they protect their hearts? That's the vulnerability that honey pots exploit.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Techies are building technology that can advance all aspects of the world — but can they protect their hearts? That's the vulnerability that honey pots exploit.

Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.

“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”

Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.

Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”

What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

“AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”

The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said.

business_items.title: US companies’ use of Chinese open weight AI draws rebuke from House chairmen
business_items.summary: An investigation led by the House Homeland Security Committee focused on the dangers of U.S. companies using lower-cost open weight AI models for certain projects.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
An investigation led by the House Homeland Security Committee focused on the dangers of U.S. companies using lower-cost open weight AI models for certain projects.

A new congressional report focused on how some American companies are embedding China-developed open weight artificial intelligence models into their tech stacks calls the trend alarming and cautions U.S. firms against the practice.

Pointing to how Huawei and ZTE technology quickly found their place in the marketplace and threatened American networks, the new report warns that if China-developed open-weight models are allowed to take root, removing them down the road will take several years and cost taxpayers billions.

Open weight models’ numerical weights and biases are made public for download.

The joint investigative report — produced by the House Homeland Security Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party — focuses on Airbnb, DoorDash and Cursor coding platform owner Anysphere as examples of companies deploying Chinese open weight models. The companies were using them for customer assistance, coding projects and taking inventory.

None of the firms immediately responded to a request for comment.

Report co-authors Reps. Andrew Garbarino (R-NY) and John Moolenaar (R-NY) drew the 50-page-long report’s findings from hearings, classified briefings, and agency advisories. The lawmakers also received briefings from DoorDash, Airbnb and Anysphere about how they integrated China-developed open-weight models into their consumer platforms, enterprise software and other systems.

“The investigation uncovered risks that American businesses, policymakers, and national security officials can no longer afford to overlook or downplay,” the report said. “While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap.”

Silicon Valley startups and Fortune 500 companies alike are adopting Chinese open-weight models because they are cheap, easily customized and work well, according to the report.

But those benefits come with significant negatives, the report said, citing federal investigators’ findings showing that Chinese developers “used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities.”

The report features 12 policy recommendations, including the imperative to build an American open-weight AI initiative, establish a standard for where models are sourced from, create an AI bill of materials, bar China-developed models from federal contract work and sensitive critical infrastructure functions and evaluate Chinese models systematically.

The report is important because it identifies and explains the risks posed by the U.S. not competing seriously in the low cost open-source model marketplace, according to Mark Montgomery, a cybersecurity expert at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

Because China is more limited in the frontier model space — dominated by U.S. firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI — its leaders have pursued a strategy to expand global dependence on their open-source AI, using the “traditional Chinese model of state policy and capital” to kill competition, he said.

“Companies and utilities, driven by bottom line resource decisions will, as always, ignore security and safety issues in pursuit of a lower front end cost,” he said. “China knows this recipe well.”

business_items.summary: The encrypted messaging app will now block those screenshots by default, following similar steps it took with Microsoft last year. The post Signal blocks Apple, Google AI screenshotting in response to ‘existential threat’ to privacy app appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Signal will block Apple and Google operating systems by default from taking screenshots of user messages to feed Siri AI and Gemini Intelligence.

Signal will now block Apple and Google operating systems by default from taking screenshots of user messages in its encrypted messaging app that feed into the companies’ artificial intelligence capabilities, the appmaker’s leadership said Friday.

Signal already had taken similar steps with Microsoft 11 last year to stop Microsoft Recall from capturing and storing messages. It will extend those limitations to Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness and Gemini Intelligence.

Signal will “restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen,” wrote the Signal Foundation’s president , Meredith Whitaker. “Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.”

“In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents ‘scan’ the information that’s on your screen,” she continued. “In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.”

The announcement follows reports that Meta’s AI agent Muse was able to access the texts of Signal messages and read them.

Signal took aim at the tech companies that produce the industry-leading operating systems.

“Sadly, OS vendors are integrating agents recklessly, w/o giving Signal and other apps good ways to block AI data access and protect you,” Whitaker wrote on social media .

“We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies — Apple, Google, and Microsoft — to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data,” she said.

Specifically, developers should have a clear way to opt-out of AI data access and processing, and they should come up with better documentation about how AI agents function, Whitaker said.

Apple, Google and Microsoft didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The firm’s parent company, Neighborhood Intelligence, said in a statement that The Container Store has “restored its website and systems following a cybersecurity incident this past weekend.”

The Container Store on Friday said it is recovering from a cyberattack that forced it to shut down its online ordering systems and limited in-store transaction processing.

The firm’s parent company, Neighborhood Intelligence, said in a statement that The Container Store has “restored its website and systems following a cybersecurity incident this past weekend.” Neighborhood Intelligence — a rebrand of Bed Bath & Beyond — purchased The Container Store in July for $150 million.

While the stores remained open throughout the week, they had to use “alternative transaction-processing procedures,” according to the statement. The Texas-founded company has about 100 stores across the U.S.

Neighborhood Intelligence said the incident only impacted The Container Store and did not affect its other brands including Bed Bath & Beyond, Overstock, buybuy BABY or Kirkland’s. Neighborhood Intelligence reported $509 million in revenue for the third quarter earlier this month, with the increases driven primarily by the acquisition of The Container Store.

The company said it hired cybersecurity experts to contain the incident and restore the affected systems. So far, it does not appear the hackers stole customer financial data, but did not address claims made by the cybercriminal group n0n, which listed the company on its leak site earlier this month.

The n0n cybercriminal group emerged in September, and cybersecurity experts say they specialize in ransomware and data extortion. The group has attacked more than 100 victim organizations and demanded hundreds of millions of dollars in ransoms.

The group initially forced victims to pay a 10% fee just to access its negotiation portal, but now forces companies to pay the full ransom before viewing any sample of the stolen information, according to SOCradar.

Allan Liska, a ransomware expert at Recorded Future, said the group launched its data leak site in late September and tried to recruit affiliates on a Russian cybercrime forum called RehubcomPro Forum in late October.

Liska said the group’s cybercriminal post claimed affiliates were instructed to only target companies that earn more than $10 million annually in revenue and were banned from attacking organizations in the Commonwealth of Independent States. The Record is an independent unit of Recorded Future.

Cybersecurity firm LevelBlue said the group has primarily targeted healthcare and pharmaceuticals but recently claimed to have troves of data from financial services companies and retail firms.

LevelBlue noted that the group has used an AI coding agent and paid AI services to write and debug its attack scripts, helping it scale operations quickly.

business_items.title: Amazon says Chinese hackers used Cairn AI tool to discover apparent zero-day during attack on university
business_items.summary: A China-linked threat actor used the open source AI penetration testing tool Cairn to persistently attack two universities, and in one case, possibly discover a zero-day bug, researchers said.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
A China-linked threat actor used the open source AI penetration testing tool Cairn to persistently attack two universities, and in one case, possibly discover a zero-day bug, researchers said.

Chinese hackers used an AI tool called Cairn to allegedly discover a zero-day while breaching several universities in Asia, according to a new report from Amazon’s Threat Intelligence team.

CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said their investigation began on September 10, when they discovered a publicly accessible server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn — an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework.

They were able to view the operational history of the platform, including previous prompts and more. The operator wrote their prompts in Simplified Chinese and the timestamps were configured to China Standard Time. The targeted victim organizations were universities in East Asia.

Moses explained that Cairn is ideal for attackers because, when given a starting point and objective in plain language, it can coordinate multiple AI agents to complete a task.

In this incident, the attacker provided IP addresses and asked Cairn to “obtain shell access” — meaning find a way to gain enough access to a system for various actions to be taken.

“Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step,” Moses said.

One of the attempts involved 148 actions taken over 16 hours that were ultimately unsuccessful, including a failed attempt at exploiting the Log4Shell vulnerability. Another failed effort saw Cairn try for more than six hours to breach university servers by testing more than 30,000 credential combinations tied to 80 real usernames.

The only successful attempt occurred when the agents discovered a vulnerability in an open-source medical imaging AI application and exploited it.

“At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched,” Moses said.

“Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.”

The attacker then used the same apparent zero-day to breach a second university.

Moses said Amazon Threat Intelligence contacted the maintainers behind the open-source medical imaging AI application and they fixed the bug that was discovered.

He added that AWS “worked with a government partner to notify the organizations about the activity.” AWS declined to name the universities or the country they are in.

Moses said the campaign stood out because of the speed and operational tempo of the AI agents.

The National Security Agency has mostly returned to business as usual after patches to a commonly-used programming language caused an internal communications network to crash for much of the week.

An NSA spokesperson said they “can confirm that we are now operating under normal conditions.”

The spy agency is operating under “normal conditions, with exceptions” today, according to a Friday morning voicemail inbox recording for its workforce.

The instructions come after three days of disruptions to NSANet, which allows employees to communicate classified information internally. The disruptions were attributed to maintenance affecting PHP, a ubiquitous programming language.

“The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in a television interview earlier this week.

Workplace interruptions also occurred at NSA Georgia. Intelligence operations at that facility, focused on the Middle East, were not negatively impacted, according to two sources familiar with the situation.

The outages also did not curtail NSA’s ability to support President Donald Trump’s trip to Asia, where he met with the leaders of China and Russia, these people said.

Administration officials have insisted the problems at the spy agency are not the result of a cyberattack and not connected to other IT woes that have impacted Microsoft products, airline travel and online banking services in recent days.

business_items.title: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online
business_items.summary: Exclusive: A simple security lapse exposed transcriptions of police interviews and bodycam footage on a cloud server without a password.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Exclusive: A simple security lapse exposed transcriptions of police interviews and bodycam footage on a cloud server without a password.

A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

According to Anurag Sen , a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”

From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records ; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system ; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts.

Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

“We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”

“We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

business_items.title: The US national cyber director is stepping down
business_items.summary: The news comes as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages, the causes of which are still unknown.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The news comes as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages, the causes of which are still unknown.

White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown.

Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director.

business_items.title: Sean Cairncross out as national cyber director
business_items.summary: During his tenure, he was involved in key administration decisions on AI security and the protection of critical infrastructure. The post Sean Cairncross out as national cyber director appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Sean Cairncross is leaving his post as National Cyber Director, with Pentagon CIO Kirsten A. Davies reportedly set to step into an acting role at the White House.

Sean Cairncross is leaving his post as national cyber director, CyberScoop has learned.

Cairncross led the Office of the National Cyber Director, which coordinates cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Though he had experience in Republican politics and national security, he lacked a technical or cyber background. His office nevertheless became involved in key administration decisions on AI security and the protection of critical infrastructure.

A source close to the White House told CyberScoop that President Donald Trump fully supported firing Cairncross from his position as he lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job.

Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will move into an acting role in the White House office, a transition that comes amid staff departures and debate over how the government should manage artificial intelligence risks.

CyberScoop has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

In a post on X , Davies thanked Trump and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller for the appointment. “Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected. Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future,” she wrote. “Under President Trump’s leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future.”

Cairncross met with technology company leaders and helped shape a June executive order that asked leading AI firms to submit new models for voluntary government testing before public release. He also was assigned to co-lead a working group tracking a nonbinding AI security commitment signed by major labs.

Cairncross advocated for collaboration between government and industry, arguing that security measures should not slow the development of AI. The administration has sought to deploy AI in critical infrastructure as a way to strengthen defenses, while lawmakers and some executives have called for stronger government guardrails. President Donald Trump has rejected new regulation.

The office’s work extended beyond AI policy. It launched a program offering cybersecurity resources to water utilities in Texas after attacks on water systems and a six-month pilot in South Carolina aimed at rural hospitals. Project Lifeline 250 connects companies, state agencies and local governments to help hospitals strengthen network defenses, keep critical care operating after an incident and replace vulnerable or aging equipment.

The projects reflect the challenges facing sectors with limited technology resources. Rural hospitals, like water utilities, often have fewer resources than other critical infrastructure operators. Federal officials have also cited healthcare as a major target for ransomware and other cyberattacks.

The leadership change at ONCD follows a period of staff turnover. Cairncross’ policy chief and senior adviser Thomas Lind joined OpenAI in October . Other senior staff members departed after the administration released its AI executive order, including an adviser involved in early policy negotiations.

The turnover comes as the administration attempts to fill other cyber leadership posts. Michael LoSapio, Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, faced a contentious confirmation hearing Thursday . CISA helps protect federal civilian networks and critical infrastructure.

Cairncross’s departure also comes after Trump administration officials blamed a spate of recent tech outages on a race to close vulnerabilities uncovered by artificial intelligence.

business_items.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
business_items.summary: Are the recent outages in the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms really a coincidence? There's actually likely something deeper going on, cybersecurity experts say.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Are the recent outages in the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms really a coincidence? There's actually likely something deeper going on, cybersecurity experts say.

It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.

Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.

The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.

Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more.

While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly.

Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related.

The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch.

The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said.

This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said.

Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote on X .

AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with.

In less technical terms, she said the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up.

When looked at this way, she said, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.”

Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said.

business_items.title: Dems call CISA nominee ‘disqualified’ after nomination hearing
business_items.summary: Michael LoSapio, the Palantir executive and Trump administration nominee for CISA, sparred with Democrats on the committee over who won the 2020 election, Jan. 6 and more. The post Dems call CISA nominee ‘disqualified’ after nomination hearing appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
CISA director nominee Michael LoSapio clashed with Senate Democrats over Jan. 6 and agency funding during a brief lame-duck confirmation hearing.

Michael LoSapio, the Palantir executive and Trump administration nominee for Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, struck a combative tone with Democrats on the Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee and took sides in several partisan disputes that are likely to complicate his path to confirmation.

LoSapio’s hearing lasted less than an hour, far less time than Congress has spent scrutinizing previous CISA nominees, as he was considered alongside a large tranche of other Trump administration nominees that Republicans are attempting to move through Congress during the lame duck session.

CISA has lacked a confirmed director for the first two years of the Trump administration, and policymakers have fresh concerns about cyber insecurity in U.S. critical infrastructure, artificial intelligence and other threats. Despite that, LoSapio and senators on the committee spent little time discussing the specifics of his vision for the federal government’s primary defensive cybersecurity agency.

When LoSapio was asked about cybersecurity issues, like how he intended to boost cybersecurity resilience of the nation in the wake of last week’s widespread outages, he said organizations should be more proactive implementing baseline protections around inventory, evaluation and patching internet-connected devices.

“It’s really important to understand the landscape of the systems you have out in the wild,” said LoSapio. “The things that you operate day-to-day, the systems that you rely on, the systems that are ancillary, and do an extensive evaluation on their vulnerabilities, whether they’ve been patched or not, how they’ve been architected and their defensive capabilities, both things we need to add and the things that exist today, as to how that maps to the threats we’re facing.”

At another point he stated that there was “more we can do across the nation” to improve security, but did not articulate beyond that. He did not commit to hiring more staff, only to evaluate the agency’s resources once confirmed.

But LoSapio also waded into several partisan debates and made comments that led Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., to state that he had “disqualified” himself from the role of CISA director by demonstrating a lack of independence from the White House.

At one point, LoSapio said he didn’t view the Jan. 6, 2021 riots led by Trump supporters on Capitol Hill as an “attack,” doubling down on the assertion when pressed repeatedly by Blumenthal. After the hearing, the social media account for Senate Homeland Security Democrats posted the exchange on X, calling on the Senate to reject LoSapio’s nomination.

“Anyone who can so easily rewrite history in service to Trump should not be leading CISA, which has critical election security obligations,” the post read.

In another exchange, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked what the impact would be on CISA if “Democrats” did not fund the agency during the lame duck session. LoSapio answered it would be “catastrophic” and likened its impact on “ordinary Americans” to calling 9-1-1 and having no one pick up. While past shutdowns have hindered agency operations, CISA and other DHS component agencies would continue to operate under emergency appropriations during a shutdown.

Later, when Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., asked about the effects of thousands of firings and hundreds of millions of dollars in cuts over the past two years, as well as the White House budget proposal that would further cut hundreds of millions next year, LoSapio said he could not assess them because he was an outsider coming to the agency.

The late nomination of LoSapio gives him little time between now and January, when a less-friendly, Democratic-majority Congress takes office, to lobby support from the lame duck Senate. His nomination will likely compete for limited floor time as the Trump administration has put forward dozens of federal nominees since the 2026 election.

Following the hearing, Punchbowl News reported that retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C. announced he would place a hold on LoSapio’s nomination.

business_items.title: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order
business_items.summary: The U.K. tribunal's ruling rejected London's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The U.K. tribunal's ruling rejected London's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.

The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information.

The Thursday ruling from the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret.

The tribunal’s ruling rejected the Home Office’s claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.

The ruling comes a year after the U.K. government reportedly demanded that Apple build a backdoor to allow U.K. authorities access to customer data anywhere in the world. Details of the so-called “technical capabilities notice,” which are issued under strict non-disclosure rules, leaked to the media, which drew ire from White House officials and U.S. lawmakers who criticized the effort , arguing that the U.K. order would put Americans’ privacy at risk.

California-based Apple refused the order, and blocked U.K. users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud, rather than comply with the demand. The U.K.’s secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud, and Apple also challenged this second order.

Prior to the ruling, Apple was legally barred from disclosing the order, even after details leaked. When reached for comment, Apple told TechCrunch that it welcomes the decision to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice.

Apple previously said that it has “never built a backdoor or master key” to any of its products or services and “never will.”

A spokesperson for the U.K. Home Office, which has yet to confirm the existence of a notice, did not respond to a request for comment.

Rights group Liberty International, which brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals, said that this is the first known time that the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order.

A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year.

business_items.title: Palmer Luckey doesn’t deny that he’s a prepper
business_items.summary: The Anduril founder said Wednesday that Americans should always have three days of food, water, and medicine — just in case.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The Anduril founder said Wednesday that Americans should always have three days of food, water, and medicine — just in case.

Defense mogul Palmer Luckey — whose $90 billion drone and weapons startup Anduril is flush with government contracts — is still the kind of guy who prepares for the worst.

During Luckey’s conversation with Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the billionaire implied that Americans should batten down the hatches in case there are rough times ahead. Luckey himself has taken steps to prepare for a potential cataclysmic event, he said.

The conversation took place against the backdrop of a series of recent large-scale outages — at Apple , at Microsoft , at the NSA , and at the Federal Aviation Administration — that have led to concerns that America may be under attack by cyberthreat actors. The government has said that this is not the case , but Luckey cryptically teased that there may be more to the story.

“Look, all the 4chan schizo posters are like 12 hours ahead of the mainstream media on this. You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough,” he said.

Sorkin also asked Luckey to expound on comments made backstage “about what might be a cyber war that seems to be going on around us.”

Luckey described a “mismatch” between the sophisticated AI-powered cyberattacks that exist today and “old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed.” He added: “I think people are going to have to pick up the pace. It’s time to start running.”

“What does that mean? Are you a prepper?” Sorkin asked.

Luckey didn’t deny the characterization. “I own a missile base 200 feet underground,” he answered, to audience laughter. “It’s a funny joke, but a missile base is actually a pretty bad way to run from the apocalypse. Everyone knows exactly where you are, and they [bases] are designed to take a hit from a nuclear weapon, a blast overpressure event.”

However, he had some qualifications on the prepper label. “The point is, like everyone should have three days of water. Everyone should have three days of dry food. If you have prescription medication, don’t go refill it when you run out. Make sure you refill it 72 hours before you run out.”

“People used to be taught this in middle school, and now everyone who remembers that is treated like a nut,” he added.

It should be pointed out that preparing for the apocalypse is not necessarily a new interest for Luckey. In 2017, a person familiar with the billionaire described him as a “prepper” and the bunker that was broached Wednesday is one of several decommissioned Cold War era underground bases that Luckey has purchased over the years. In 2024, he revealed that his massive video game collection is housed in one of them.

business_items.title: Palmer Luckey warns AI-powered cyberattacks are outpacing defenses: ‘It’s time to start running’
business_items.summary: The Anduril co-founder says outdated technology is leaving systems vulnerable to a new wave of AI-enabled attacks.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The Anduril co-founder says outdated technology is leaving systems vulnerable to a new wave of AI-enabled attacks.

AI-powered cyberattacks are moving faster than outdated technology systems can defend against them, Palmer Luckey warned at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. Addressing the recent spate of tech outages, the Oculus founder and Anduril Industries co-founder argued that older systems are struggling to keep pace with the new hacking capabilities enabled by AI and warned it was time to quicken the pace of securing our defenses.

“We’re seeing the natural effects of a lot of these advanced AI tools allowing for the creation of various exploits,” he said.

While government officials largely attributed the latest set of technical issues to companies rushing to patch their systems to protect against the new vulnerabilities AI has discovered, Luckey focused on the underlying security challenges facing organizations using outdated technology.

Luckey explained that U.S. adversaries are currently exploiting the mismatch between new attack capabilities and our defense capabilities. These attacks are being carried out for both strategic and financial reasons, and North Korea was particularly involved, he added.

The interviewer, Andrew Ross Sorkin, noted that U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance had canceled his appearance at the Times’ conference this week because of the recent tech outages, saying he now had to attend meetings about the matter.

Given the situation, Sorkin asked Luckey how worried we should be about all this.

“It depends on how well prepared you are,” was Luckey’s answer. (He then ominously warned, “You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough.”)

The tech executive argued that AI could ultimately give defenders the upper hand, but they’d have to move more quickly.

“In the long run, the advantages are going to accrue to the side that is most effectively using AI for defense,” Luckey said. “With the people who say that everything can be hacked — they are right, for now. That actually may be the case with certain new techniques that are coming along. But as of right now, there’s a mismatch between the attackers who are very fast-moving and using technology and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed,” Luckey continued.

“And I think … people are going to have to pick up the pace,” he said. “It’s time to start running.”

business_items.title: Consensus mounts that tech outages were fueled by patching of AI-discovered vulnerabilities
business_items.summary: But cyberattacks aren’t directly to blame, Trump administration officials said. The post Consensus mounts that tech outages were fueled by patching of AI-discovered vulnerabilities appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Federal officials and lawmakers say a rush to patch AI-discovered vulnerabilities, rather than cyberattacks, likely fueled recent major tech outages.

Cyberattacks almost certainly aren’t responsible for the procession of major tech outages over the past week, Trump administration officials say — but there’s a growing sense that patching fueled by a race to close vulnerabilities uncovered by artificial intelligence was a contributing factor.

The top Democrats on the House and Senate intelligence committees are among those observing that the rise in vulnerability discoveries resulting from AI are at least partially to blame for tech service interruptions like those ranging from the aviation ground stop to incidents with major communications and banking systems, rather than the direct result of hacking.

“What appears to be happening instead is a consequence of how quickly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape,” Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said Tuesday. “AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change.”

And Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., said Wednesday that the trend is likely to continue.

“It is possible that the increased pace of vulnerability discovery and patching could cause more frequent outages, but the breakneck pace of patching we have seen in recent months is vital to shore up the security of all IT infrastructure,” he said. “Disruptions in networks, whether through internal errors or outside attack[s], are a fact of life, but we can do much more to be prepared and resilient.”

At a House Homeland Security Committee hearing Wednesday, Trump administration witnesses repeatedly cited patching, rather than hacking, as a cause of the outages, although they didn’t specify that the patches were a result of AI unearthing vulnerabilities.

“We are in an environment where the rate of patching, the rate of upgrading of systems, is increasing,” said Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence. “That is a result of the advancements in compute, and in applications.”

But lawmakers were more explicit. The Washington Sun reported that Wednesday that during Hill briefings, industry and government officials cited patching in response to AI-discovered vulnerabilities as the cause . Rep. James Walkinshaw, D-Va., responded at Wednesday’s hearing to Clayton testifying that the incidents were “unrelated” to one another.

“The recent tech outages are not coincidences, and they are connected to cybersecurity,” Walkinshaw said. As cyberattacks are “exploding,” everyone is “frantically patching systems.”

Walkinshaw noted that as attacks have been on the rise, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has had its personnel and budget dramatically cut.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that despite the cuts, CISA is “able to meet our mission right now because of new technology that has come in,” but he didn’t say what technology he meant.

Mullin also said he didn’t have any update for lawmakers about the pace of CISA hiring, as committee members from both sides of the aisle pressed him to increase personnel at the agency.

Clayton and Mullin, as well as FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia, repeatedly said that so far, there remains no evidence that malicious cyberattacks had anything to do with the outages. They also said that there was no sign that cyber adversaries were seizing on the time necessary to implement patching to conduct attacks.

business_items.title: Senate Republicans advance FCC nominee, slate of cyber bills
business_items.summary: Confirmation would give Republicans a 3-1 majority on the FCC. Meanwhile, the fates of multiple bipartisan cyber bills are in limbo after Democrats no-showed the markup hearing. The post Senate Republicans advance FCC nominee, slate of cyber bills appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Senate Commerce Committee Republicans advanced Danielle Thumann Severs' FCC nomination and several tech and cybersecurity bills amid a Democratic boycott.

Republicans in the Senate Commerce Committee advanced the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs to serve as a commissioner at the Federal Communications Commission.

Alongside Severs’ nomination, the GOP majority also voted favorably on a slew of tech and cybersecurity bills. But Democrats – who will wield the majority gavel in January – boycotted the hearing, throwing the fate of the bills into question, even as many had bipartisan sponsorship.

If confirmed, Thumann Severs would give Republicans and chair Brendan Carr a 3-1 majority on the commission, with Biden administration holdover Anna Gomez the only remaining Democrat. The Trump administration has not moved to fire Gomez as it did two Democratic commissioners on the Federal Trade Commission last year. But he also broke with precedent by declining to name a Democratic-appointee alongside Thumann Severs to round out the five-member commission.

In a hearing room that sat half-empty on the Democratic side, committee chair Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas defended the decision to move forward with Thumann Severs’ nomination after resounding losses in the midterm elections.

“What it should tell us is that the Democrats have zero intention of processing any of the president’s nominees,” Cruz said. “We are heading into two years of total destruction, total war, partisan warfare is what the Democrats are promising us.”

He argued President Donald Trump is not legally required to nominate FCC commissioners in pairs, and is merely to elect no more than three members of the same party. The nomination of Thumann Severs, he claimed, is “consistent with that requirement.”

He also suggested that President Trump had demonstrated a desire for the commission to remain bipartisan by declining to fire Gomez after the Supreme Court upheld his right to do so to FTC commissioners last year .

CyberScoop has reached out to Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee for comment. On Tuesday committee member Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., accused Thumann Severs of not being forthcoming about her role in support of Carr’s media bias investigations.

Republicans on the committee also advanced multiple tech and cybersecurity-related bills.

The COLLUDE Act , sponsored by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., would create a private right to sue social media companies that make content moderation decisions based on government requests. Specifically, the bill would strip liability protections under Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act for social media companies, opening them to private lawsuits from individuals if their account or post bans

As Missouri Attorney General, Schmitt led a lawsuit over the Biden administration’s information sharing with social media companies around COVID-19 and election disinformation. That case eventually reached the Supreme Court, where the majority concluded that the communications were non-coercive and that social media companies have their own, constitutionally-protected incentives for moderating speech on their platforms.

Under the Trump administration and Carr, the FCC has gone considerably further than the Biden administration in attempting to police political speech over the public airwaves, opening investigations into broadcast media organizations that have aired interviews with Democratic opponents and at times likening their perceived disagreement with the federal government as evidence of broadcasting undue ideological bias. Thumann Severs served as Carr’s senior counsel prior to being nominated as FCC commissioner.

When moving forward Thumann Severs’ nomination earlier in the meeting, Cruz and other Republicans gave only verbal commitments to hold the FCC accountable for its mission to protect free speech.

Another bill, the Telecommunications Cybersecurity and Resilience Act , sponsored by Cruz and Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., would establish a telecommunications cybersecurity working group at the Department of Commerce that would be charged with developing industry best practices around cybersecurity and develop criteria for independent third-party cybersecurity certifications and assessors.

business_items.title: It’s NGINX’s turn to cause vulnpocalypse headaches
business_items.summary: Researchers just dropped five NGINX exploits, including one that chains an HTTP/2 bug with a kernel flaw to seize the machine behind the web server. The post It’s NGINX’s turn to cause vulnpocalypse headaches appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
F5 patched five NGINX vulnerabilities after researchers released exploits, including an HTTP/2 flaw (CVE-2026-123007) chained to seize host servers.

Security researchers disclosed five vulnerabilities Tuesday in NGINX, the web server software that handles traffic for roughly a third of all websites, each with a working exploit. The most severe allows an unauthenticated attacker to run code on the server from anywhere on the internet, and in tests the researchers chained it with a separate Linux kernel flaw to take over the machine hosting the server entirely.

F5, the company behind NGINX, released fixes Tuesday and published an advisory classifying the worst of the flaws, an integer underflow tracked as CVE-2026-123007, as critical, scoring 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS scale.

The problem sits in HTTP/2, the protocol NGINX uses to carry many requests over a single connection. HTTP/2 uses a credit system: the client grants the server permission to send a fixed amount of data. When a client cancels a request while its response data is still waiting to be sent, NGINX hands back that unused credit without checking whether the total now exceeds the protocol’s maximum. A later check subtracts the inflated number from the maximum using unsigned arithmetic, which cannot go negative, so the calculation wraps into an enormous value. That broken number is eventually treated as a negative response length, producing a memory buffer whose end pointer sits before its start, and a memory copy that spills outside its boundaries.

Rapid7 researcher Stephen Fewer, credited in F5’s advisory along with Wiz Research , Xint.io and Ikotas Labs, built a working exploit against a NGINX 1.31.8 container with HTTP/2 and TLS enabled.

The attack has practical limits: it requires roughly 128 gigabytes of HTTP/2 traffic, most of it control frames carrying no actual data. The demonstration took two-and-a-half minutes on a fast local network, but would need about two minutes over a 10-gigabit link and 17 minutes over 1 gigabit. Because NGINX closes connections after an hour by default, a network slower than about 300 megabits per second cannot finish the attack in time. The exploit also leans on a specific optimized memory-copy routine in the GNU C Library, selected on x86-64 chips with certain AVX-512 features. Rapid7 said other exploit methods may exist but none are currently known.

The other flaws affect different NGINX features, including reverse proxying over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, combinations of the resolver and mirror directives, and mail proxying. Wiz Research, working with Ikotas Labs, Metnir and Rapid7, independently found two of the same flaws and documented one of them, a use-after-free bug, in reverse-proxy setups where connection slots run low.

Xint, which found four of the five flaws with an automated testing harness and no human guidance, went furthest. A researcher pointed the harness at about 50,000 lines of NGINX code; 90 minutes later it produced high-severity findings, and a working exploit followed within 10 minutes. The team then chained the HTTP/2 bug with a separate flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP networking code to reach root, the highest privilege level on the host. F5 said its cloud services are still being evaluated while BIG-IP and F5OS products were found not vulnerable.

“When we used Xint to scan NGINX, we didn’t know what to expect, since it’s a mature, widely deployed codebase that’s undergone years of scrutiny,” Brian Pak, co-founder and CEO of Xint, said in a statement to CyberScoop. “Others have targeted NGINX with AI pentesting, but none found this critical bug, which is a testament to our team and the engineering expertise that’s gone into our AI harnesses. We’re grateful for the collaboration with project maintainers to get a patch released quickly.”

Xint’s Shodan snapshot found 98.9% of 11.94 million version-identifiable NGINX hosts running affected releases, though that counts versions, not confirmed exposure, since it does not show whether each server accepts HTTP/2 or has received a backported fix. Wiz, which validated its findings with AI models, connected the convergence of separate teams on the same long-hidden bugs to AI’s improving ability to trace memory-safety flaws, a capability available to defenders and attackers alike.

The findings come as cybersecurity researchers continue to find critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software. Just 24 hours ago, researchers disclosed a critical flaw in Java , one of the world’s most used programming languages, that could let an attacker take over servers without a password. Last month, researchers found a host of similar vulnerabilities , leading to some labeling the month as “Black October.”

business_items.title: More banks say customers using AI agents are on their own — even if they get hacked
business_items.summary: Citi is the latest major financial institution to put the breaks on personal finance AI agents.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Citi is the latest major financial institution to put the breaks on personal finance AI agents.

Citibank, the third largest commercial bank in the United States, changed its terms of service this week, telling customers who use third-party AI tools for personal finance that anything that goes wrong is their problem — even if they get hacked.

AI agents, ranging from frontier lab models to purpose-built personal finance tools, can be given the credentials to your bank account and other online financial portals, with the idea that they can analyze spending and investment decisions, offer advice, and even handle transactions and bill payments.

But financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants.

“As third-party AI tools become more widely available, we want customers to understand the risks associated with sharing banking credentials or authorizing those tools to access their accounts,” a Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch. “We recently updated our Online User Agreement to provide greater clarity about those risks and to reinforce that customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.”

JPMorgan and Bank of America , the two largest banks in the country, announced similar policies last month. And PNC, the eighth largest bank, changed its terms today.

Citi’s update goes beyond telling customers that they are responsible for anything their agents may do; it also informs them that if the AI tool leaks their credentials or is hacked, the customer will be responsible for anything hackers do with their account. Banking giant Citizens similarly emailed its customers this week, warning that they are also on the hook for anything their AI assistant does, according to an email seen by TechCrunch.

As AI startups look for more revenue, breaking into personal finance presents an attractive opportunity for companies to add value for customers and wet their beaks in the stream of fees generated by the sector. But if consumers are already leery of sharing their email or chat records with an AI agent, bank and brokerage accounts offer a new trust challenge.

Anthropic’s approach is telling: The personal finance tool it launched earlier this month is explicitly billed as “read-only” and “can’t move, manage, or invest your money.”

Beyond cybersecurity concerns, banks also view efforts to enter their franchise as a competitive threat. Markets shuddered briefly in reaction to the prospect of AI tools making it easier for consumers to avoid unnecessary fees or low-interest deposit accounts that pad bank margins. But if AI agents become an important way to interact with financial decisions, banks will fight to control that pathway. Citi’s terms note that AI agents it provides can be used by customers without worrying about additional liability.

The reaction by banks is part of a broader trend among businesses of all stripes: AI labs promise that their agents will revolutionize the way people engage with a variety of service providers, then the service providers say “hold on a minute.” We’ve seen it in everything from car-hailing to food service , and how these relationships play out will help determine which AI investments pay off.

business_items.title: British hackers face prison for GTA 6 data breach and crypto thefts
business_items.summary: Two British hackers face lengthy prison sentences for hacks that broke into the Grand Theft Auto gamemaker and for stealing millions in crypto.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Two British hackers face lengthy prison sentences for hacks that broke into the Grand Theft Auto gamemaker and for stealing millions in crypto.

Two British hackers are facing lengthy prison sentences for separate hacks as part of their roles in long-running, prolific cybercriminal hacking groups. The two are accused of hacks that stole millions of dollars in cryptocurrency and leaked pre-release footage from Grand Theft Auto VI.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years by a U.S. court after he was extradited to the United States in 2025. Buchanan was accused of stealing at least $11 million in cryptocurrency from dozens of companies as part of a phishing scheme. The attacks would impersonate IT helpdesks and call up unsuspecting employees and trick them into giving over their credentials, which the hackers would use to break in and steal cryptocurrency.

Meanwhile, Arion Kurtaj, 21, from Oxford, England, has pleaded guilty to several cyberattacks that he carried out while a teenager. One hack included the theft of data and extortion of Rockstar Games, the maker of Grand Theft Auto VI, which was released Wednesday after several delays .

Kurtaj was previously ordered by a U.K. court to be detained indefinitely after deeming him unable to stand trial due to his autism diagnosis and his perceived high hacking risk to the public. But U.K. authorities, tasked with charging Kurtaj with cybercrime offenses, confirmed Monday that he had admitted to several hacks, including leaking footage of the long-awaited video game, and would subsequently face a public trial.

U.K. authorities confirmed earlier reporting that Kurtaj hacked several companies, including while he was confined to a hotel amid police protection from rival criminal gangs. The authorities said Kurtaj used an Amazon Fire TV stick to hack the companies, which breached his bail conditions.

Both Buchanan and Kurtaj were members of overlapping cybercriminal groups, dubbed 0ktapus, Lapsus$, and later Scattered Spider . These prolific hacking gangs mostly consist of teenagers and young male adults, lending to the term “advanced persistent teenagers,” whose focus and motivations were to steal as much money as possible through various cyberattacks.

Over the years, the hackers were collectively responsible for hundreds of cyberattacks targeting big companies, including Coinbase , DoorDash , Mailchimp , and Nvidia .

By late 2024, both U.K. and U.S. authorities say they had indicted five of the hackers whom they believed were key members of the hacking groups, including Buchanan. The U.S. Department of Justice said this week that Buchanan is the fifth and final defendant to be sentenced in this case.

business_items.title: Government tech debt is a national security risk
business_items.summary: With 80% of federal IT budgets spent maintaining aging legacy systems, fragmented government networks are struggling to defend against AI-accelerated cyberattacks from foreign adversaries. The post Government tech debt is a national security risk appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Federal agencies spend $80 billion annually maintaining legacy IT systems, leaving fragmented networks vulnerable to Chinese and Russian cyberattacks.

In August, the Federal Bureau of Investigation announced that it detected and disrupted another Chinese state-sponsored cyberattack targeting U.S. critical infrastructure — the latest in a series that includes the 2025 PlugX malware incident, the 2024 Flax Typhoon hack and the 2023 Volt Typhoon operation. The severity and frequency of these attacks should raise alarms because they show a pattern of America’s adversaries looking for any possible weakness in our sensitive systems to exploit, and in many cases cooperating together to do so.

These attacks are often aimed at the federal government’s own networks, and they are all too often successful. The incoming House and Senate cyber leaders will need to assess and address this vulnerability fast.

The math isn’t on the government’s side. Cyber adversaries only have to be right once, whereas defenders must be right across every system, program and vendor. Unfortunately, the very way that the federal government contracts and manages critical systems makes the job of its cyber defenders much more difficult.

Federal systems are often cobbled together over decades, often with unpredictable budgets, shifting missions and procurement rules that favor incremental fixes over true modernization. The outdated technology is often easy to identify. The more dangerous aspect of the problem is the complexity embedded in federal management efforts, ensuring that addressing the challenge will be hard.

Under the guidance of the Office of Management and Budget and the General Services Administration, federal agencies routinely run three or four generations of systems simultaneously — legacy databases sitting beneath cloud environments, with managed service providers and internal teams each touching different layers, often without a shared map of what connects what. Security is often added later, after missions have changed, the platforms expanded, and new compliance requirements emerged.

Federal information technology spending exceeds $100 billion annually, according to a 2025 R Street Institute report , with as much as 80 percent dedicated to operating and maintaining existing systems. The government spends this $80 billion a year simply to keep old systems secure while adversaries invest in new technologies and techniques to infiltrate them. Adversaries now have access to agentic AI systems to automate their reconnaissance efforts, accelerate exploitation of known vulnerabilities and move through supply chains before a patch cycle completes.

The fragmentation of federal networks and defenses makes it easier for foreign adversaries to penetrate systems, and it poses a significant strategic risk. The federal government may not have the network resilience to continue to operate in a crisis or contingency with China or Russia. Congress is starting to pay attention, but because cyber investment is less tangible than a new fighter jet or missile system and is spread across dozens of authorization and appropriation subcommittees in each chamber, it often takes a back seat.

Congress should treat federal technology modernization as a security imperative with the same urgency it has applied to traditional Defense Department weapons acquisition.

Agencies need procurement pathways that allow trusted security technologies to be adopted without multiyear acquisition cycles. Vendor contracts should define accountability clearly enough that, after a breach, the party responsible can be identified in hours rather than weeks. Platform duplication should also be reduced where it expands the attack surface without adding operational capability.

Weapons acquisition reform is focusing on delivering capabilities to warfighters faster and at lower cost. Federal cybersecurity infrastructure acquisition should be held to the same standard. Faster modernization would make government harder to penetrate and quicker to recover. Government tech debt is a strategic vulnerability, and our adversaries are already exploiting it.
