business_items.title: A vulnpocalypse bug worthy of attention: Researchers disclose critical flaw in Java with help of AI
business_items.summary: Oracle shipped a patch this week for the flaw, which a short string of letters can trigger to corrupt memory in Java and hand attackers control of the servers running it. The post A vulnpocalypse bug worthy of attention: Researchers disclose critical flaw in Java with help of AI appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Researchers at Calif used AI to uncover Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical OpenJDK memory-corruption flaw patched by Oracle on Tuesday.

Security researchers on Tuesday published details of a critical flaw in Java, one of the world’s most used programming languages, that could let an attacker take over servers without a password.

The group behind the find, Calif Research, said AI coding tools did much of the work. Oracle Corp. shipped a fix the same day it released a November update covering 652 flaws across its product line.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and nicknamed Java4Shell . It is a memory-corruption bug: code that writes data where it does not belong, which can crash a program or, at worst, let an attacker run their own commands. The buggy component is the Base64 decoder in OpenJDK, the free Java runtime that underpins software across banking, aviation and telecommunications, and that, by Calif’s count, runs at 90% of Fortune 500 companies.

Calif rated the flaw 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS scale, where anything above 9 counts as critical. The group said an unauthenticated attacker, one who needs no username or password, could corrupt a server’s memory, read nearby data in a manner similar to the 2014 Heartbleed bug, and escalate that access into full control.

The bug lives in an unusual place: hand-written processor instructions that OpenJDK uses to make Base64 decoding faster. The optimization runs only on chips that support a feature set called AVX-512; ARM64 systems are unaffected. Calif found the decoder breaks on a specific input: 64 ‘A’ characters followed by a single equal sign, the padding mark Base64 uses to round out incomplete data.

The code then miscalculates a length and writes 64 bytes into a buffer, a small block of memory meant to hold as few as 50, overwriting whatever sits next to it. The program rejects the bad input afterward, but the surrounding memory is already damaged.

On its own, that corruption usually crashes the program. Calif showed that an attacker who carefully arranges what sits in the surrounding memory, a technique known as heap grooming, can turn the corruption into control of the server.

The group reported unauthenticated code execution in widely used products including Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and PingFederate, and demonstrated a working break-in against Keycloak, a widely used open-source login system. Authenticated execution, requiring a valid account, was shown in Kafka, Solr and Elasticsearch. Researcher samczsun showed Java programs can also be compromised simply by connecting to a malicious server.

OpenJDK published a security advisory Tuesday, and Oracle shipped patched Java builds Tuesday afternoon.

The find adds to a fast-growing catalog of vulnerabilities surfaced with AI. Calif said researcher Quang Luong found the bug in about an hour auditing OpenJDK with OpenAI’s Codex, for under $200 in computing tokens, and that AI agents produced most of the group’s exploit chains nearly on their own. It was the group’s second major AI-assisted find in recent weeks, after last month’s disclosure of php2shell.

In its write-up, the group called this the era of “the centaur hacker, part human, part AI,” and said the hunt for the bug felt like “looking for copper and found gold.”

Calif also framed the bug as a byproduct of software’s shared complexity: the AVX-512 speedup shipped with every copy of Java though few programs need it, so an optimization became a critical risk for all. The group said there is no universal exploit and each target requires tailored steps, and it is withholding product-specific exploit details until users have had time to upgrade.

No exploitation in the wild had been reported as of this article’s publication, and none of the CVEs related to the issue have been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerability list. However, the agency published a notice calling for a patch late Tuesday. With Calif researchers already proving that unauthenticated RCE is possible in widely deployed apps, researchers tell CyberScoop the likelihood of real-world exploitation is high, especially given how fast attackers can leverage artificial intelligence.

“We’re talking about a vulnerability in one of the most widely used software runtimes in the world, with initial exploit development taking just a few hours,” said Gal Elbaz, co-founder and CTO of Oligo Security. “That doesn’t mean every Java application is vulnerable or that exploitation will be straightforward. Attackers still need to account for specific hardware, runtime configurations, and application behavior. But the technical barriers are clearly surmountable, and organizations should treat this as a serious exposure that requires compensating controls capable of blocking exploitation while patches are rolled out.”

business_items.title: Google joins the tech outage trend by announcing it’s not having one
business_items.summary: With tech outages seemingly everywhere, Google took the unusual step of announcing that Gmail is working just fine, actually.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
With tech outages seemingly everywhere, Google took the unusual step of announcing that Gmail is working just fine, actually.

Was Google feeling a little left out of the recent wave of tech outages? The company took to X on Tuesday to announce that its Gmail service is actually running just fine. In a post, the company said it was not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption and reminded users they could always check Gmail’s real-time status on its online dashboard .

As it turns out, the company was trying to head off reports of a Gmail outage that began circulating on X on Tuesday around the same time that Apple was seeing a number of verified outages of its own . While some posts on the social network suggested Gmail was experiencing a disruption, others said they were not having any problems.

The concerns seemed to stem from an X post by Downdetector, a crowdsourced website where users can report service disruptions themselves and see if others are having problems. Downdetector is not an official source for verifying or understanding the true scope of internet outages, and as people become more concerned about possible cyberattacks, the site’s data may become less valuable over time if every minor glitch and hiccup is reported as an “outage” by non-technical users.

The fact that Google had to announce it was not having an outage speaks to the growing anxiety around the reliability of major tech services. Over the past week, Apple and Microsoft experienced outages, an FAA network failure led to a nationwide ground stop, and some banks and airlines also reported disruptions.

However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox Business Network’s “The Claman Countdown” on Tuesday that the U.S. is not currently facing coordinated cyberattacks. He told the outlet, “We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here.”

Instead, Clayton attributed the rise in issues to businesses patching their systems. The patching may be a downstream effect of AI, as newer models have become increasingly adept at uncovering previously unknown vulnerabilities. “They’re upgrading them, they’re putting patches in place,” he said, adding that this is happening at “a much larger scale” than before.

As a result, some of the systems are “not coming back as expected in all cases,” he added.

business_items.summary: Agency leaders and federal contractors are mulling over how to best adapt the new protections to older, legacy technology and address gaps in visibility over federal encryption protocols. business_items.details:
GSA has begun running post-quantum encryption on employee PIV cards as federal agencies race to meet an accelerated 2030 transition deadline.

As federal agencies revise their strategies for implementing post-quantum encryption by President Donald Trump’s new 2030 deadline , agency leaders and federal contractors are mulling over how to adapt the new protections to older, legacy technology and address gaps in visibility over federal encryption protocols.

Dan Pomeroy, deputy associate administrator at the Office of Technology Policy at the General Services Administration, said his agency focused first on the smart Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards that grant employees access to GSA facilities, computers and the authority to sign official documents.

Pomeroy said agency technologists ran new post-quantum encryption algorithms directly onto the card chip, issued new credentials, and built the surrounding policies, certifications and hardware security modules to support the transition.

Post-quantum cryptography tends to require larger keys and signatures, along with a fast, reliable network connection to process larger amounts of data. That could be a problem for assets like satellites, which have weaker connections. But in many cases, agencies can switch to newer algorithms using the same systems, data and devices already in use throughout the government.

“That work demonstrated that quantum-resistant credentials are not theoretical, they are achievable with the cards we have today, the technology we have today,” said Pomeroy Tuesday at FedTalks presented by FedScoop.

Pomeroy also said the government constantly needs to test for bugs and interoperability issues. His agency works with contractors to make sure they use post-quantum algorithms “from the start” and bring the necessary infrastructure to support the agency’s encryption efforts.

An executive order issued earlier this year moved the mandatory federal deadline for completing the post-quantum transition from 2035 to 2030. Major private-sector organizations like Google have set similar internal timelines of 2029 for their own encryption switchovers, citing similar concerns.

The order cut by more than half the time agencies were originally given to transition their public key encryption. While national security officials have cited threats like “harvest now, decrypt later” in pushing for faster adoption, experts say that encryption switchovers are often measured in decades.

Vanessa Hunt, general manager for federal markets at IBM, said many federal agencies have “blind spots” in their network, particularly in areas where “the sensitivity of the data outlives the approach protecting it.”

Additionally, encryption protocols are often spread across different datasets, identities, infrastructure and networks, making it difficult to map everything that needs to be upgraded.

“I think the biggest blind spot right now is just the visibility,” said Hunt. “I think it’s easier to know where our sensitive data lives, it’s less easy to know where the cryptography that protects it is.”

business_items.title: How CISA is prioritizing companies for talks about security improvements
business_items.summary: CISA acting director Nick Andersen made his remarks after speaking at FedTalks, presented by FedScoop. The post How CISA is prioritizing companies for talks about security improvements appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
CISA has identified about 100 vital critical infrastructure companies for targeted cybersecurity talks to harden systems under its CISA 2030 strategy.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has identified approximately 100 companies that own critical infrastructure for talks on hardening their systems because of how vital they are to the nation, CISA acting director Nick Andersen said Tuesday.

That figure does not cover everyone CISA wants to speak with, because those companies have so many interdependencies with other firms, he said. And the conversations are going to vary wildly from company to company, he told CyberScoop.

“For the initial workstream, we’re probably talking about around 100 companies,” Andersen said after speaking at FedTalks, produced by FedScoop. “We want to be focused on being able to gather what are those lessons learned that are most appropriate coming out of it, what works and what doesn’t, and the problem with each one of those different companies.”

To generate the list, CISA went through an intergovernmental Homeland Defense Working Group that identified companies that provide functions deemed most important to the economy, public health and safety, national security and defense critical infrastructure.

Then, Andersen said, the agency overlaid five to six years of intelligence about what cyber adversaries appeared to value most, such as where they were pre-positioning or where their research and development budgets were going. Companies that appeared on both lists became the targets for “initial engagement,” which also meant involving the right sector risk management agencies.

So hypothetically, if the decision is that a particular port is especially important, CISA would talk to the port operator. “But I also need to have a conversation with their energy provider, with their telecommunications provider, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera,” he said.

In his FedTalks speech Andersen said the ideal is to have conversations that include IT and operational technology providers, along with cybersecurity providers. He said the goal is to advance the agency’s “CISA 2030” strategy, which focuses on resilience, minimum viability and related priorities.

“It’s going to continue to result in several significant, important conversations over the coming weeks and months about, what does it mean to appropriately invest?” Andersen said. “What does it mean to collaborate with one another on that longer-term resilience as we move forward? That’s going to have to be a collective effort across our communities.“

So far, he said, the conversations have been productive.

“A lot of this has also included things like CI-Fortify assessments with those companies, which have been really really good conversations for us to be able to have around, what does it mean to be able to plan for isolation and recovery?” Andersen said.

Andersen, and other Trump administration officials, have spoken in recent months about the need to be selective in how they prioritize vulnerabilities and hacking targets.

business_items.title: Proton’s Lumo, a privacy-focused alternative to ChatGPT and Claude, arrives on desktop
business_items.summary: Proton's new Lumo Desktop app for Windows, Mac, and Linux lets users automate tasks across files and connected apps, with granular controls over what its AI can access.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Proton's new Lumo Desktop app for Windows, Mac, and Linux lets users automate tasks across files and connected apps, with granular controls over what its AI can access.

Proton , the privacy-focused tech company offering alternatives to Google’s and Microsoft’s tools for email, productivity apps, password management, cloud storage, and more, is now bringing its AI app Lumo to personal computers. On Tuesday, the company launched Lumo Desktop for Windows, macOS, and Linux, allowing users to leverage its AI to carry out local tasks on their computer involving connected apps, personal files, and other automations.

The app is designed to offer users more control over their personal data, as consumer AI technology becomes focused more on AI agents that can perform tasks on users’ behalf, rather than just answering questions.

Already, the major model makers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others, offer desktop tools for working with their AI technologies, but doing so invites increased risk to users’ personal data . Only this week, for instance, Apple announced it was addressing those privacy concerns with tightened security settings for apps that request Full Disk Access, as the AI desktop apps do.

Proton’s idea is to offer a set of tools that let its AI access connected apps, files, and folders and automate tasks, but with more personalization over how much access the AI has. The company says users can choose which actions the AI agent takes that will need to request their approval, and it vows that the conversations and information from connected apps and files are never used to serve personalized ads or train AI models.

The new app includes a variety of connectors that support local tools, like file-system access, shell execution, and browser content fetching, as well as Proton’s email app and other third-party services, including Confluence, Dropbox, and Jira.

The connectors also support local and remote MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, which AI agents use to access external data sources.

Proton says that users can decide for each connector which actions Lumo can perform automatically, which require approval, and which are blocked entirely. Users can also turn individual tools off from the Tools menu in their conversation.

In addition, users can set up their own scheduled tasks, where each has its own set of permissions, in terms of what can be handled automatically and what requires approval.

Proton notes that it uses encryption to ensure that only users can read their chat history, not the company. The company also says it keeps no server-side logs, and the limited data it does store is protected under Swiss privacy law. The data is hosted on European infrastructure, outside the scope of the U.S. CLOUD Act , which specifies how law enforcement agencies access data held by cloud service providers.

The company says it’s investing in its infrastructure, with its first Nvidia B300 cluster built on Open Compute Project (OCP) standards now going live in Switzerland.

Similar to other AI apps, Lumo’s desktop app supports Skills, which lets users save instructions, templates, and reference files that Lumo can reuse across their conversations. (An earlier version of this, Custom Lumos, will now be migrated to the Skills format.)

business_items.summary: Three months since introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corba has raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Three months since introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corba has raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA.

Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.

The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP , a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js , the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.

Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin , as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

business_items.title: Cyber giant Infoblox confirms security incident after hackers access ‘company information’
business_items.summary: The cybersecurity and automation giant said it's working with outside investigators to understand the scale of the breach.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The cybersecurity and automation giant said it's working with outside investigators to understand the scale of the breach.

Cybersecurity and automation giant Infoblox has confirmed a cybersecurity incident, during which hackers accessed company information through one of its technology vendors.

Infoblox is a privately held cyber giant that provides companies cybersecurity and networking services, such as domain name resolution and identity and user access management.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Infoblox told TechCrunch that the company is “investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor.”

“We immediately activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident and are working with leading outside cybersecurity experts to investigate the facts, understand the scope and address any confirmed risks.”

TechCrunch has learned that the data breach involves a vendor that provides SharePoint data migration services, according to a notification sent by Infoblox about the breach, two people with knowledge of the incident told TechCrunch.

One of the people said sensitive customer data was taken in the breach.

According to public internet records seen by TechCrunch, Infoblox hosts much of its files, emails, and infrastructure with Microsoft, including a SharePoint server, which TechCrunch confirmed is accessible through Infoblox’s single sign-on provider. SharePoint is web-based software that companies use to share and host internal files and documents.

Infoblox has not named the third-party migration vendor that was hacked, but one person with knowledge of the incident said that Infoblox has terminated its work with the vendor.

The company’s spokesperson did not comment on this, but added that the company has “no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved” in the breach.

Infoblox would not say how many customers were affected by the incident, or if the company is aware at this time. The company also did not say, when asked, if it had been contacted by the hackers and if they had made any demands.

business_items.title: Apple reveals new Mac security controls as AI agents raise privacy risks
business_items.summary: Following an October announcement, Apple has detailed new permission controls, warnings, and transparency features coming to macOS 27.3 to address risks posed by AI agents and other apps.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Following an October announcement, Apple has detailed new permission controls, warnings, and transparency features coming to macOS 27.3 to address risks posed by AI agents and other apps.

As promised last month , Apple on Monday announced changes to Mac security controls designed to protect users’ data from the growing popularity of AI agents and their apps’ demand for “full disk access.”

“Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk,” Apple warned in its blog post aimed at app developers.

Unlike AI chatbots that simply answer questions, agents run on a user’s device where they can take actions across the operating system, files, and apps on the user’s behalf.

While the tools can be useful, Apple has grown concerned about the increased risks to users’ data and privacy that these AI agents introduce. At the same time, the company has been benefiting from sales of Mac minis and Mac Studio computers that AI early adopters have been purchasing specifically to run their local AI models.

To balance these competing interests, Apple said in October that it would revise some of its security settings around Mac apps. The announcement followed two notable incidents involving AI agents. In one, a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app read their private messages without consent; a separate report from Wired cited a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app that could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data.

For starters, it’s splitting up Device Control and Data Access into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The changes are designed to help users better understand that selecting the first option means overriding built-in security protections.

To streamline configurations, Apple says there will now also be a single method for granting permissions that involves selecting the requested app from a list. The company will also introduce new guidance encouraging users to grant access only to the specific apps that need it when they enable the System & App Protection Override setting. Similar guidance will appear when users enable Full Disk Access to allow an app to access their folders.

The company will also provide users with “increased visibility into the wide range of data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are granted,” the blog post notes.

Another change will give users more granular control over when an AI agent or app can gain access by allowing users to configure their apps to ask for permission every time access is needed. While arguably tedious and a potential obstacle to true automation, the feature could allow users to experiment with local AI without giving the agent carte blanche.

There will also be a new transparency indicator that appears when an app is controlling another app through the System & App Protection Override option.

The changes, which are arriving with macOS 27.3, don’t appear to prevent Mac users from installing and running AI agents or other apps that ask for higher levels of access. Instead, they give users more nuanced options, control, and information about the choices they’re making.

Apple advises app developers to adjust their onboarding processes to account for the new changes and suggests that their apps learn to “gracefully handle having access to only a limited set of folders or apps.”

Developers of apps that request Full Disk Access for disk backup or to provide assistive technologies can request exceptions to the new rules (which Apple calls “entitlements”) to preserve the same functionality they offered before the macOS 27.3 update.

business_items.title: Uber says hackers stole information on close to 150,000 driver’s licenses during data breach
business_items.summary: The ride-sharing giant said driver's license information stored by AI cloud company Fireworks AI was stolen during a security incident.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The ride-sharing giant said driver's license information stored by AI cloud company Fireworks AI was stolen during a security incident.

Uber is notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers.

In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California and Iowa , the ride-hailing giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data.

The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider.

The stolen data includes affected drivers’ names, addresses, dates of birth, and driver’s license numbers.

TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open-weight AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets.

Online productivity startup Notion and AI coding startup Cursor have both confirmed that they had data stolen during the Fireworks hack.

In Uber’s case, the company said it had alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its Fireworks environment, but because the hackers used Fireworks’ own internal credentials, “no alerts were triggered.”

When reached for comment, an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch: “The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” and deferred our questions to Fireworks.

A spokesperson for Fireworks confirmed that the company identified a security issue involving unauthorized access to some of its systems, which affected customer data, but the spokesperson did not address our questions about the incident.

Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs. No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft.

In a notice filed with Oregon’s attorney general, Uber said it notified 149,346 people in total that their information had been taken in the breach at Fireworks.

TechCrunch previously reported that Uber has notified drivers in California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and South Carolina. We’ve also seen data breach notices filed in Texas and Vermont.

When asked by TechCrunch, Uber’s spokesperson did not say how many drivers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident.

It’s unclear if the number of affected drivers is expected to rise, and Uber did not respond to a follow-up email sent Monday.

business_items.title: FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
business_items.summary: The FBI says that the open source hacking tool was used in cyberattacks targeting a U.S. IT giant and the South Korean financial industry.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The FBI says that the open source hacking tool was used in cyberattacks targeting a U.S. IT giant and the South Korean financial industry.

The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.

In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory , the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.

Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up.

In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”

The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.

Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.

The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.

The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.

The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.

A spokesperson for ConnectWise told TechCrunch that the company does not have the visibility to confirm the number of affected environments as cited by the FBI.

Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.

“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen.

A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.

After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller and Manager Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, formerly SD-WAN vSmart, and Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, formerly SD-WAN vManage, contain an authentication bypass vulnerability could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to bypass authentication and obtain administrative privileges on an affected system. This vulnerability exists because the peering authentication mechanism in an affected system is not working properly. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending crafted requests to an affected system. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to log in to an affected Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller as an internal, high-privileged, non-root user account. Using this account, the attacker could access NETCONF, which would then allow the attacker to manipulate network configuration for the SD-WAN fabric.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Authentication Bypass Vulnerability

CVE-2021-1435, previously associated with the exploitation events, is no longer believed to be related to this activity.

items.details:
Hackers are exploiting CVE-2026-131914, a critical unpatched Idunno.AntiCsrf flaw enabling unauthenticated RCE in ASP.NET WebForms.

Cybersecurity researchers have urged users to discontinue using a legacy ASP.NET anti-CSRF library named Idunno.AntiCsrf ("Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll") following the discovery of a critical vulnerability that has been exploited in the wild.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-131914 , carries a CVSS score of 9.3 out of 10.0. The issue affects versions 0.9.1.0 and 0.9.1 Beta, and relates to an insecure deserialization vulnerability in the Idunno.AntiCsrf.AntiCsrfModule HTTP module.

Idunno.AntiCsrf is a third-party ASP.NET IHttpModule designed to provide double-submit cookie Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection for ASP.NET WebForms applications. The open-source project is currently defunct and has not been updated since December 2008.

At its core, the problem stems from the fact that the module deserializes untrusted CSRF form token data using an unkeyed .NET System.Web.UI.ObjectStateFormatter instance without cryptographic MAC or signature verification when handling incoming HTTP POST requests to ASP.NET WebForms (System.Web.UI.Page) endpoints.

This behavior, in turn, can allow a remote attacker to achieve arbitrary remote code execution (RCE). Google's Mandiant division has given the vulnerability a "High" exploitability assessment, adding that exploitation hinges only on a single HTTP POST request with no prior authentication or valid CSRF token.

LDB, Genwei Jiang, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, Brian Bahtiarian, and Lucas Kossack of Google Cloud and Mandiant Incident Response have been credited with discovering the flaw earlier this month.

"A remote attacker can supply any non-empty value in the configured CSRF cookie alongside a Base64-encoded .NET ObjectStateFormatter gadget chain in the configured CSRF form field to execute arbitrary code in the context of the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe), resulting in complete compromise of the web application server," Google-owned Mandiant said in an alert issued last week.

Google's threat intelligence team did not disclose any further details related to the activity. The Hacker News has contacted Google, and we will update the story if we hear back.

In the absence of an official patch, organizations still using the library are advised to discontinue its use and replace it with an actively supported anti-CSRF alternative such as follows -

ASP.NET WebForms Page.ViewStateUserKey combined with MAC-verified/encrypted ViewState on postback forms

"Audit all ASP.NET Web.config files and bin/ directories for references to Idunno.AntiCsrf or AntiCsrfModule, and review IIS logs for anomalous POST requests to .aspx endpoints returning HTTP 302 or HTTP 500 with elevated cs-bytes (where logged)," Google said.

"Environments with evidence of exploitation should rotate all secrets stored in Web.config and applicationHost.config (including <machineKey> keys, encryption keys, and database credentials) and inspect webroots for unauthorized files."

items.title: Microsoft confirms Windows printing issues affecting Forcepoint users
items.summary: Microsoft confirmed printing issues on systems running Forcepoint DLP software after installing the KB5132043 November 2026 Windows 11 hotpatch. [...]
items.details:
Microsoft confirmed printing issues on systems running Forcepoint DLP software after installing the KB5132043 November 2026 Windows 11 hotpatch.

Microsoft confirms Windows printing issues affecting Forcepoint users

Microsoft confirmed that some Forcepoint users may experience printing issues after installing the November 2026 Windows 11 hotpatch.

In a Friday service alert seen by BleepingComputer, Microsoft said this known issue affects only systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later.

According to Microsoft, the printing problems stem from a compatibility issue between the KB5132043 Windows hotpatch update and the Forcepoint DLP Endpoint Agent endpoint data loss prevention solution.

"After installing the November 2026 Windows hotpatch update (the Originating KBs listed above), devices running Forcepoint DLP Endpoint Agent might experience printing issues," Microsoft said. "Affected users might find that the print option is greyed out or encounter errors when selecting a printer. This issue occurs because the Print Spooler service fails to start."

While a fix is not yet available, Forcepoint has shared a temporary workaround for its customers in this support document , which can be accessed after signing in to the Forcepoint support portal.

Last week, Microsoft also warned that the KB5132043 hotpatch is causing installation and launch issues affecting Office and third-party applications on Windows 11 systems.

These two known issues should not affect systems with the standard November 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates, only those that have installed the hotpatch updates pushed through Microsoft's Windows Autopatch , a cloud-based enterprise service designed to automate Windows and Microsoft 365 updates.

However, as the company confirmed two weeks ago, the November 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates may also break printing for users trying to print documents with complex formatting on server (Windows Server 2016 or later) and client (Windows 10 or later) devices.

Microsoft unveiled Windows Autopatch in April 2022, saying it would be available for free to customers with a Windows 10/11 Enterprise E3 license or greater starting in July 2022. Windows Autopatch was made available in public preview in early June 2022 and reached general availability in July 2022 .

In March, it announced that it would turn on hotpatch security updates by default for all eligible Windows devices managed through Microsoft Intune and the Graph API on systems with the May 2026 Windows security updates installed.

One month later, Microsoft fixed a Windows Autopatch bug that deployed driver updates restricted by administrative policies on some Autopatch-managed Windows devices belonging to customers across the European Union.

items.title: Hackers Exploited GL.iNet Cloud Flaw to Install Malware on Routers and KVM Devices
items.summary: Hackers exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud remote management service to install malware on some customer routers and KVM devices, the maker of travel routers and remote-access KVM hardware said in a security notice updated today. The company identified and fixed the flaw on Friday and blocked the access the attacker used, so devices can no longer be infected through this route.
items.details:
Hackers exploited a GL.iNet GoodCloud flaw to infect routers and KVMs. Security firmware removes identified malware, but persistence concerns remain.

Hackers exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet 's GoodCloud remote management service to install malware on some customer routers and KVM devices, the maker of travel routers and remote-access KVM hardware said in a security notice updated today.

The company identified and fixed the flaw on Friday and blocked the access the attacker used, so devices can no longer be infected through this route. The cloud-side fix does not remove malware from devices that were already infected, so owners still need to check their hardware and install the security firmware listed today.

A KVM is a small device used to control a computer remotely as if sitting in front of it. The company is still investigating whether computers attached to infected KVMs were affected.

It has not said how many devices were infected, when the attacks began, or how its cloud service was breached. It is emailing customers it identifies as affected, but owners do not need to wait for a message to act.

A model missing from the firmware table below is not necessarily unaffected, the notice says, and owners should not install firmware meant for another model.

RemoteToHome Consulting, a security consultancy that examined the incident on routers it manages, says in its incident investigation that it verified a root-level reverse shell on one of its GL-AXT1800 routers.

The shell started on Friday evening and connected to 170.39.226[.]219, and two more owners reported the same shell on the same model and firmware, 4.8.3, with GoodCloud switched on.

On GL-MT6000 routers, the same shell command ran but the connection never completed. On other routers the firm manages, a one-off command searched for files linked to a KVM implant and reported the result to the same address.

The shell leaves no files behind, and its traces vanish when the device restarts, per the firm's reverse-shell analysis . The process marker the vendor published was absent on the router with the verified shell.

After the researchers filed an abuse report late last week, the hosting provider told them it had suspended the server behind the address and preserved its data.

The shell arrived through the GoodCloud client software on the router itself, according to the firm's technical analysis . A handler in that client takes two values from a cloud message and runs them as root through the shell without checking them. The vendor has not confirmed that finding.

The unchecked code has been in the firmware since at least December 5, 2024, when it appeared in a GL-MT3000 release. It runs whether or not AstroWarp, the SD-WAN feature it belongs to, is in use, and its presence since 2024 does not mean attacks began then.

The researchers reported a second, separate weakness in the cloud client to the vendor yesterday and are withholding details until it is fixed.

One KVM owner described an infected GL-RM1 in an owner's report . Starting on Thursday, the device downloaded a script and two programs from 66.245.219[.]252, looked up the copycat domain gl-inet[.]top, and scanned the local network.

items.title: AI-Assisted Cyberattacks Trigger Unauthorized Payments at Indian Banks and Fintech Firms
items.summary: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has warned that threat actors are carrying out artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyber attacks targeting information and communication technology (ICT) assets in the country. This unsanctioned activity has resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers
items.details:
CERT-In warns AI-assisted attacks are abusing trusted business workflows to trigger unauthorized payments at Indian financial and technology firms.

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has warned that threat actors are carrying out artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyber attacks targeting information and communication technology (ICT) assets in the country.

This unsanctioned activity has resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts.

"In the observed incidents, attackers targeted business records and approval processes to carry out unauthorized transactions through otherwise legitimate systems," CERT-In said in an advisory last week.

The incidents have been found to include the following methods -

Abuse of business applications and service provider-operated workflows, as opposed to direct exploitation of payment-related APIs.

Modification of business records or approval relationships, followed by the use of legitimate payment processes.

Use of trusted systems and established approval procedures to process unauthorized transactions without raising any alert.

Exploitation of security blind spots in independent verification, reconciliation, and review of changes to business records..

CERT-In did not reveal how much money had been improperly paid out, or by whom. The activity has not been attributed to any specific threat actor.

The agency also said that separate threat-hunting has uncovered the use of AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks (AOFS) across enterprise, technology, government, academic, and research sectors to conduct the following actions -

Automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services, and potential attack paths.

Rapid generation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including by analyzing software patches and related technical information.

Using a cluster of AI agents to undertake intrusion tasks, such as reconnaissance and privilege discovery, in parallel.

Modifying scripts, requests, and attack methods in response to errors, blocked attempts, or information returned by targeted systems.

items.title: CISA flags critical Cisco RCE flaw as actively exploited in attacks
items.summary: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned federal agencies that attackers are now exploiting a recently patched critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability in the wild. [...]
items.details:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned federal agencies that attackers are now exploiting a recently patched critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability in the wild.

CISA flags critical Cisco RCE flaw as actively exploited in attacks

​The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned federal agencies that attackers are now exploiting a recently patched critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability in the wild.

Cisco Expressway Series devices are enterprise collaboration gateways (deployed as virtual machines or physical hardware appliances) that connect internal voice and video systems with outside networks and remote users via a secure connection.

Tracked as CVE-2026-76466 , this security flaw stems from the use of hard-coded credentials and a failure to fully validate client certificates, enabling unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute arbitrary operating system commands as root on affected Cisco Expressway-C and Cisco Expressway-E devices configured in a cluster.

"An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands," Cisco said in late October, when it released security patches to address the issue.

While Cisco says that its Product Security Incident Response Team (PSIRT) is not aware of active exploitation in the wild or publicly available proof-of-concept exploits targeting this vulnerability, CISA tagged it as actively exploited on Friday.

The cybersecurity agency also added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Tuesday and ordered US Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to secure their systems within three days, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04.

Although BOD 26-04 targets only federal agencies, CISA urged all network defenders, including private-sector security teams, to prioritize patching this flaw to block ongoing attacks that may target their networks.

"These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise," it warned.

While CISA has yet to share details on these ongoing attacks, Russian cybersecurity company F6 said on Thursday that it spotted attackers using an unnamed AI assistant to successfully exploit CVE-2026-7646 and gain remote command execution with full root privileges on Internet-exposed Cisco Expressway devices.

"The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices. Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network," F6 security researchers noted.

"After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure. They used custom Python scripts designed to scan the network, discover accessible SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and explore GitLab repositories in order to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive information."

Two weeks ago, CISA also flagged a high-severity Cisco BroadWorks vulnerability (CVE-2026-20320) as actively exploited in attacks and ordered federal agencies to patch their systems by November 24.

According to threat intelligence firm Malbear Labs, a Chinese-speaking threat actor abused CVE-2026-20320 in autonomous AI attacks targeting a European telecommunications provider and 13 organizations that used its data centers and cloud infrastructure.

The system must be rebooted for this update to take effect.

Red Hat recommends treating all kernel errata as security-relevant. Given the kernel's fundamental role, any bug has a higher chance of impacting system security, even if that impact only becomes clear after a fix is published. Therefore, Red Hat prioritizes delivering fixes that improve our customers' overall security posture.

Because of this proactive approach, a patch may be associated with a CVE assignment at a future date. Retroactive CVE assignments are always documented in the corresponding errata and on Red Hat's CVE pages. We strongly advise against delaying updates, as doing so may leave your system exposed when protections are already available.

items.title: Hackers exploit GL.iNet cloud flaw to infect routers, KVM devices
items.summary: GL.iNet has confirmed that hackers exploited a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services to install custom malware on customers' routers and KVM devices, with some affected users reporting backdoors and reverse shells giving remote access to infected devices. [...]
items.details:
GL.iNet has confirmed that hackers exploited a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services to install custom malware on customers' routers and KVM devices, with some affected users reporting backdoors and reverse shells giving remote access to infected devices.

Hackers exploit GL.iNet cloud flaw to infect routers, KVM devices

GL.iNet manufactures networking equipment, including home and travel routers, as well as KVM devices that allow users to access and control computers remotely.

Its GoodCloud platform allows customers to remotely manage supported devices, including accessing and controlling computers and servers connected to its KVM products.

In a security advisory published on November 20, GL.iNet confirmed that an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services to access devices and install malicious software.

"The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident," the company said .

"Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. These measures do not remove malware from devices that were already infected."

GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were impacted, or whether information was stolen from compromised devices.

The company is also investigating whether computers connected to infected KVM devices were compromised.

GL.iNet recommends that customers check their devices for signs of infection and install the latest security firmware, even if no malware is detected.

The company's initial instructions told customers to look for a process running as crond -i /tmp/.log , which GL.iNet said was an indicator of compromise.

While the cloud vulnerability has been fixed, GL.iNet says stable firmware updates containing additional security fixes for both routers and KVM devices are scheduled for release on November 22, 2026.

For KVM devices, customers can follow the company's firmware upgrade guidance , which recommends version 1.10.3 or later for the RM10, RM1, RM1V2, RM1PE, and RM4PE, version 1.10.3 beta or later for the RM10RC, and version 1.8.7 or later for the RMQ1.

Router owners should install the latest security firmware for their specific model as soon as it becomes available.

items.title: Cleverbridge warns hackers stole credit card numbers, CVVs in data breach
items.summary: E-commerce platform Cleverbridge is warning that hackers breached its systems and stole customers' payment card information, including credit card numbers and CVV security codes. [...]
items.details:
E-commerce platform Cleverbridge is warning that hackers breached its systems and stole customers' payment card information, including credit card numbers and CVV security codes.

Cleverbridge warns hackers stole credit card numbers, CVVs in data breach

Cleverbridge provides e-commerce services to software and SaaS companies, allowing them to sell products, process payments, and manage subscriptions.

The company lists numerous technology brands as its customers, including Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Sony, and Parallels. However, it has not disclosed which businesses' customers were impacted by the breach.

In a new page about the security incident, Cleverbridge says it detected unauthorized activity on November 4, 2026, and temporarily took systems offline to contain the breach.

"All systems were brought back online on 4 November 2026; however, our investigation subsequently determined that a third party copied payment card data stored on our platform," reads the security incident disclosure .

Cleverbridge began notifying affected customers on November 20, warning that hackers had stolen payment card details used to make purchases through its platform.

While its public disclosure confirms the theft of payment card data, it does not specify which card details were stolen, instead referring affected customers to their individual notifications for more information.

However, a breach notification shared with BleepingComputer reveals that the stolen information includes payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV/CVC security codes.

"Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes the payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC)," reads the notification.

"Note however that no other personal data (for example your name, contact or billing details) were copied. The affected card ends in XXXX."

BleepingComputer redacted the last four digits of the affected payment card.

The company has not disclosed how the attackers gained access to its platform, how long they remained in its systems, or how many customers were affected by the breach.

Of particular concern is the theft of CVV/CVC security codes, which are used to verify payment card transactions.

items.title: Signal to block Siri, Gemini AI from capturing chats on iOS, Android
items.summary: Signal has announced new protections that block screenshots on iOS 27 and prevent AI assistants from capturing conversations on supported Android devices. [...]
items.details:
Signal has announced new protections that block screenshots on iOS 27 and prevent AI assistants from capturing conversations on supported Android devices.

Signal to block Siri, Gemini AI from capturing chats on iOS, Android

The protections are designed to stop Siri and Gemini, the AI assistants built into iOS and Android, from accessing private conversations while performing tasks for users.

The change comes after Signal introduced a feature in May 2025 that blocks Microsoft's controversial Recall screenshot-capturing feature on Windows 11.

"We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen," Signal's president, Meredith Whittaker, said in a blog post .

Whittaker says OS-level features such as Siri's Onscreen Awareness and Google's Gemini Intelligence can capture chat content as it appears on the app's screen, putting potentially sensitive private data outside Signal's control and exposing all conversation participants.

Signal says its engineers spent months figuring out how AI systems access app data, designing targeted protections to block all extraction pathways verified through reverse engineering.

However, Signal warns that AI agents could still access conversations through other methods, which Whittaker describes as "an existential threat to Signal."

She explains that AI agents could access conversation data in multiple ways, as they are now embedded deep in operating systems, leaving apps vulnerable and with limited options for protecting users.

The most notable example is macOS, where Signal says it's currently unable to provide any screenshot-blocking protection.

For macOS 27 users, Signal recommends adding the app to the Excluded Apps list under System Settings > Siri to prevent Siri AI from proactively accessing message content.

For this reason, Signal calls on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to fully disclose, through detailed documentation, all potential access mechanisms and give app developers a clear way to opt out of AI access across screens, files, notifications, and APIs.

Signal did not provide specific app version numbers for the new protections but says they are automatically activated when possible.

Signal recommends that users upgrade to the latest available version and go to Settings > App Security to check that Block Siri AI is enabled on iOS.

items.title: OpenRouter Drops 3 Providers After Researchers Catch Months of Prompt Theft at AI Hosting Firms
items.summary: Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week. items.details:
Attackers stole AI prompts from three inference providers, prompting OpenRouter to remove 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility.

Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week.

Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention , the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored.

OpenRouter , a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said.

The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said.

The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it.

The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack.

The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls.

One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server.

On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections.

"A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer.

The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found.

The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys.

One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt.

A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab.

items.details:
Ghostscript flaw CVE-2026-125396 allows crafted files to escape its sandbox and execute server commands through common file-processing apps.

A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it.

Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly.

Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396 , was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks.

Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses.

The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files.

The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering.

Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor.

WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index .

Artifex , which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report . The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory .

WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes . That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other.

The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced.

Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system:

SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress

SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and 16.1: fix in progress

items.title: Rackspace Spot breach let hackers access customer Kubernetes secrets
items.summary: Rackspace warned customers that hackers breached its Rackspace Spot cloud platform using compromised credentials, allowing them to deploy unauthorized workloads and access Kubernetes secrets in customer clusters. [...]
items.details:
Rackspace warned customers that hackers breached its Rackspace Spot cloud platform using compromised credentials, allowing them to deploy unauthorized workloads and access Kubernetes secrets in customer clusters.

Rackspace Spot breach let hackers access customer Kubernetes secrets

Rackspace Spot is a cloud platform that allows organizations to deploy and manage containerized applications using Kubernetes.

The company disclosed the breach in a notification sent to affected customers and obtained by BleepingComputer, stating that attackers accessed parts of the platform on November 17, 2026, between approximately 00:20 and 22:00 UTC.

Rackspace says it learned of the intrusion on November 18 after receiving a customer report and confirmed that the recipient's organization was affected that same day.

"On 17 November 2026 (about 00:20–22:00 UTC), an unauthorized party used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot," reads the notification.

According to Rackspace, the attackers were able to act as legitimate users in some customer organizations, allowing them to create pods in Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes.

Kubernetes Secrets store sensitive information such as passwords, authentication tokens, and API keys that can be used to access databases, cloud services, and other systems.

Rackspace warned that the attackers could have read any Secret stored in an affected user's clusters, as well as any Spot API tokens or refresh tokens held by that user.

The company says it has since revoked affected tokens and sessions, removed the unauthorized pods, rotated keys, and strengthened access controls and monitoring.

Affected customers have been instructed to reissue their Spot API tokens, replace refresh tokens used in automation tools, download fresh Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their cluster Secrets.

Rackspace also advised customers to analyze logs associated with databases, container registries, Git repositories, cloud storage, and third-party services dating back to November 17 to identify possible abuse of exposed credentials.

The company shared the following indicators of compromise associated with the attack:

Suspicious Kubernetes pod and object prefixes: i1, glm-, and probe

items.title: Microsoft Entra Connect Health flaw exploited to steal tenant data
items.summary: Microsoft is warning organizations that it suffered a data breach after attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Entra Connect Health service to gain unauthorized access to administrator email addresses and tenant configuration information. [...]
items.details:
Microsoft is warning organizations that it suffered a data breach after attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Entra Connect Health service to gain unauthorized access to administrator email addresses and tenant configuration information.

Microsoft Entra Connect Health flaw exploited to steal tenant data

Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud-based monitoring service that allows administrators to monitor the health, performance, and alerts of their on-premises identity infrastructure through the Microsoft Entra admin center.

According to a security notification sent to admins yesterday and shared on Reddit , Microsoft discovered the vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API on November 9, 2026, after it was first introduced on July 23.

An investigation determined that the flaw was exploited, allowing unauthorized parties to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially modify Connect Health monitoring configurations.

"On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes," Microsoft said in the notification.

Email addresses belonging to tenant technical contacts and administrator accounts.

Tenant IDs, display names, initial domain names, country codes, and regional information.

Microsoft Entra license tiers and directory synchronization status, including whether synchronization was enabled and the last synchronization timestamp.

An expired certificate previously used to register Connect Health agents with a Microsoft internal service that was decommissioned in late 2024.

Microsoft says the expired certificate was no longer in use but remained in Connect Health storage and was still returned by the API.

However, the company says the vulnerability did not expose user passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, valid cryptographic keys, on-premises server and Active Directory topology details, or Azure subscription information.

Microsoft deployed a server-side fix on November 19 to prevent further exploitation and reviewed available telemetry to identify unauthorized API calls affecting customers. The company finished its investigation on November 20 and began notifying affected organizations.

Microsoft has not disclosed how many organizations were impacted, but more than a dozen administrators have reported receiving the notification in the Reddit post.

items.title: BADBOX botnet returns with record-breaking 40 billion daily ad requests
items.summary: The BADBOX malware found in a broad range of generic Android TV boxes has returned to large-scale ad-fraud operations following last year's disruptions. [...]
items.details:
The BADBOX malware found in a broad range of generic Android TV boxes has returned to large-scale ad-fraud operations following last year's disruptions.

BADBOX botnet returns with record-breaking 40 billion daily ad requests

The BADBOX malware botnet has returned following last year's disruptions, generating a record 40 billion fraudulent advertising bid requests per day through infected Android-based devices.

According to HUMAN's Satori researchers, who uncovered and disrupted the latest variant, BADBOX 3.0 had grown into the largest documented ad-fraud operation by daily bid request volume.

BADBOX was first discovered in early 2023 on a T95 Android TV box bought on Amazon. In December 2024, Germany's cybersecurity agencies warned that the botnet had infected tens of thousands of devices .

In March 2025, a large-scale disruption operation took place where HUMAN and Shadowserver cut off more than 500,000 BADBOX 2.0 devices from their control servers, while Google removed 24 apps that spread the malware from Google Play.

Google later sued the botnet's operators , saying the BADBOX 2.0 had infected over 10 million Android-based devices by April 2025.

However, the previous disruptions didn't stop the BADBOX operators from rebuilding the botnet and setting new records for daily fraudulent advertising bid requests.

"At its height, BADBOX 3.0 accounted for roughly 40 billion bid requests a day and more than 4% of all CTV traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform," reports HUMAN .

"BADBOX 3.0's volume was more than three times the volume of the previous record holder, VASTFLUX, and represents a larger peak than the last five years' worth of published Satori investigations combined."

The modus operandi remains the same: infecting cheap phones, tablets, and streaming TV boxes running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) with malware that performs ad fraud and traffic proxying.

The malware performs ad fraud by playing video ads in hidden windows while impersonating legitimate streaming apps to make the requests appear legitimate.

HUMAN also observed fraudulent server-side ad insertion (SSAI) requests that tricked advertisers into believing ads were played on streaming devices, even though no actual device or video ad was involved.

A proxying module also enrolled infected devices in one of 11 residential proxy networks without the owners' knowledge or consent.

One of those networks, PXYEDGE, was identified as the rebranded successor to IpMoYu, a residential proxy service previously linked to BADBOX 2.0.
